article_title: Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics
citation: Zhu Z, Luo C and Li L (2026) Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics. Front. Psychol. 17:1844703. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1844703
title: PPO reinforcement learning generative policy converting evaluation signals into adaptive exercise tracks
description: The generative module uses Proximal Policy Optimization with a clipped-surrogate objective to convert teaching evaluation indicators into reward functions and adjust generation parameters in real time. The state is the learner's performance feature vector plus current exercise difficulty; actions are a three-dimensional continuous vector controlling tempo multiplier (0.7–1.3), dynamic range compression (0.5–1.5) and note density factor (0.6–1.4). The per-step reward Rt = −Dt + αΔDt balances current accuracy against progress with α = 0.3, each step corresponding to 30 s of practice; PPO used clipping coefficient 0.2, γ = 0.99, GAE λ = 0.95, and training stopped when validation reward did not improve for 30 consecutive episodes.
requirements: The skill deficiency probability matrix output by the big data analysis module as input to the generative network
A decoder with temporal memory (recursive neural network with attention-based mask decoding) to synthesize MIDI sequences and waveform parameters
constraints: PPO was selected partly because clipping prevents destructive policy changes that could collapse the artistic logic of generated songs during excessive parameter updates
target_learning_goals: generated practice exercises matched to the learner's real-time skill progression
examples: Each 60-min session constituted one episode of 120 time steps, with episodic return the sum of per-step rewards over the 120 steps
key_sources: Zhu Z, Luo C and Li L (2026) Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics. Front. Psychol. 17:1844703. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1844703

article_title: A Longitudinal Investigation of the Role of Quantity and Quality of Child-Directed Speech in Vocabulary Development
citation: Rowe Meredith L. (2012). A longitudinal investigation of the role of quantity and quality of child-directed speech in vocabulary development. Child development. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3440540/
title: PPVT-III as an independent standardized measure of receptive vocabulary
description: The Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test (PPVT-III; Dunn & Dunn, 1997) served as the vocabulary outcome measure, administered by a researcher at child ages 30, 42, and 54 months. The authors chose it because "the PPVT is a widely used measure of vocabulary skill and, importantly, because it provides data that is independent from the parent-child interaction." This independence allowed the study to test whether caregiver input predicts vocabulary skill measured outside the interaction, avoiding contamination from concurrent caregiver speech. Raw scores were converted to age-appropriate standardized scores based on published norms.
requirements: Researcher administration separate from parent-child interaction
Age-appropriate standardized scoring based on published norms
constraints: Two children did not complete the PPVT at 30 and 54 months, reducing sample size to 48 at those ages
examples: Administered at 30, 42, and 54 months in home visits; mean normed scores rose from 96.2 at 30 months to 110.4 at 54 months
key_sources: Rowe Meredith L. (2012). A longitudinal investigation of the role of quantity and quality of child-directed speech in vocabulary development. Child development. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3440540/

article_title: An analysis of the empirical research on SL/FL teaching and learning based on positive psychology: a systematic literature review.
citation: Jia, M., Xin, T., Lina, Z., Baoling, Z., & Li, M. (2025). An analysis of the empirical research on SL/FL teaching and learning based on positive psychology: a systematic literature review. BMC Psychology, 13, 319. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-02576-5
title: Positive psychology frameworks (PERMA, EMPATHICS, Broaden-and-Build, Control-Value) structure SL/FL learning research
description: The review identifies several theoretical frameworks used to study positive psychology in SL/FL learning, including Seligman's PERMA model ("P: positive emotion. E: engagement. R: relationship. M: meaning. A: accomplishment"), Oxford's EMPATHICS model, the Broaden-and-Build Theory, and Control Value Theory. These frameworks are used both to design interventions (e.g. a 14-week PERMA-based listening and speaking intervention) and to organize the review's analysis of how positive emotions and traits influence language learning outcomes.
requirements: Studies applying these frameworks require structured intervention designs (e.g. the 14-week PERMA intervention) and measurement instruments such as the Foreign Language Enjoyment Scale and Grit Scale.
constraints: The review notes the reliance on self-report questionnaires may introduce bias, and most studies are cross-sectional, limiting causal inference.
target_learners: SL/FL learners at primary and secondary level
examples: A 14-week intervention using Seligman's PERMA model on students' listening and speaking showed significant improvements compared to traditional teaching methods.
key_sources: Jia, M., Xin, T., Lina, Z., Baoling, Z., & Li, M. (2025). An analysis of the empirical research on SL/FL teaching and learning based on positive psychology: a systematic literature review. BMC Psychology, 13, 319. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-02576-5

article_title: Effective Game Based Citizenship Education in the Age of New Media
citation: Chee, Y.S., Mehrotra, S. and Liu, Q. (2013). Effective Game Based Citizenship Education in the Age of new Media. The Electronic Journal of e-Learning, Vol 11 Issue 1, pp16-28. https://www.ejel.org
title: Performance–play–dialog (PPD) design model for game-based learning
description: The PPD design model views learning through the lens of performance, cultivated through play and dialog, mirroring Dewey's action–reflection dialectic. The article states: "In prior work, we proposed the performance –play–dialog (PPD) design model for game-based learning (Chee, 2011)." In the model, play is instantiated by students playing Statecraft X, where learning to be is experienced in the first person through role taking, and dialog is teacher-facilitated classroom conversation prompting reflection and sense making. The model raises the desired outcome standard to VIP: values, identity, and performance.
requirements: Dialog must take place in the classroom during scheduled lesson time and be facilitated by a teacher
The game must provide a first-person role-taking experience rather than third-person learning about
constraints: The model was proposed in prior work by Chee (2011) and is applied here to the citizenship education context
examples: The Statecraft X curriculum instantiates the model: students play the game as governors outside class and engage in teacher-facilitated dialogic sessions during class time.
key_sources: Chee, Y.S., Mehrotra, S. and Liu, Q. (2013). Effective Game Based Citizenship Education in the Age of new Media. The Electronic Journal of e-Learning, Vol 11 Issue 1, pp16-28. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1012864

article_title: Using Advance Organizers to Enhance Pupils' Achievement in Learning Poetry in English Language
citation: Mary Muiruri, Patriciah Wambugu, Kuria Wamukuru. (2016). Using Advance Organizers to Enhance Pupils' Achievement in Poetry in English Language. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(31). https://www.iiste.org
title: Pupils' Poetry Achievement Test (PPAT)
description: The Pupils' Poetry Achievement Test (PPAT) is a researcher-constructed instrument used as both pre-test and post-test to measure pupils' achievement in poetry. It "contained 15 objective type questions", was "validated by experts and also pilot tested to ascertain the reliability coefficient", yielding "a reliability coefficient of 0.76", which the authors judge suitable against Gall, Borg & Gall's threshold of 0.7. For the post-test the PPAT was reorganized "to take care of pupils being test-wise".
requirements: Expert validation and pilot testing to establish reliability
constraints: Post-test version was reorganized to reduce test-wiseness effects
target_learners: class seven primary pupils in Kenya
target_learning_goals: measuring achievement in poetry in English language
examples: Administered as pre-test to E1 and C1 before a three-week treatment, then as post-test to all four groups
key_sources: Mary Muiruri, Patriciah Wambugu, Kuria Wamukuru. (2016). Using Advance Organizers to Enhance Pupils' Achievement in Poetry in English Language. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(31). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1122519

article_title: Powerpoint as a Potential Tool to Learners' Vocabulary Retention: Empirical Evidences from a Vietnamese Secondary Education Setting
citation: Ta Thanh Nam & Lap Q. Trinh. (2012). PowerPoint as a potential tool to learners' vocabulary retention: Empirical evidences from a Vietnamese secondary education setting. li-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 2 No. 4, October - December.
title: PPT-enhanced vocabulary lessons
description: PPT-enhanced lessons are the study's experimental treatment: traditional textbook-based lessons that retain the same teaching aids but add multimedia slides. The article defines them by contrast: "traditional lessons" are "textbook-based lessons with teaching aids such as blackboard, chalk, and printed pictures", while "PPT lessons include the same elements but are designed to include multimedia." In the Vietnamese EFL setting, PPT accompanies the blackboard and textbook in one lesson, using text, sound, pictures, video and animated effects to present new lexical items.
requirements: Equipment and room requirements: functioning computers, data projectors or LCD panels, electricity and projection screens, as the article advises teachers to consider before teaching
constraints: Out-of-date computers can slow lessons with many images; lack of electricity or projection equipment may limit PPT lessons to certain rooms
target_learners: Grade-10 EFL students in Vietnamese secondary education
examples: The experimental group's lessons used PPT alongside blackboard and textbook; control lessons used blackboard, chalk and printed pictures only
key_sources: Ta Thanh Nam & Lap Q. Trinh. (2012). PowerPoint as a potential tool to learners' vocabulary retention: Empirical evidences from a Vietnamese secondary education setting. li-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 2 No. 4, October - December. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1070209

article_title: Sketch Strategy of Knowledge in Physics Learning and Its Influence on Metacognitive
citation: Bunga D. Amin, Helmi Abdullah and Jasruddin D. Malago. (2018). Sketch strategy of knowledge in physics learning and its influence on metacognitive. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2017.3293
title: Level-graded physics problem sets (PPM levels 1–3) distinguished by the number of linked cases and equations
description: The article uses a three-level problem scheme introduced by Abdullah (2014) that distinguishes test difficulty "based on the number of equations needed to solve the problem". Level-1 items need a single embedded formulation (S = vt); level-2 items connect two cases with different conditions; level-3 items link three cases and require deep thought across multiple concept schemes. The pattern was applied to linear motion at constant speed with escalator problems at each level.
requirements: Problems must be graded by the number of linked cases and equations rather than by surface topic
constraints: The article applies the pattern only to linear motion at constant speed in this study
examples: The three escalator problems printed in the article: a 20 m escalator at 0.5 m/s (level-1), a child walking up and down with velocity twice the escalator's (level-2), and a combined walking-and-moving case (level-3)
key_sources: Bunga D. Amin, Helmi Abdullah and Jasruddin D. Malago. (2018). Sketch strategy of knowledge in physics learning and its influence on metacognitive. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2017.3293

article_title: Evaluation of the impact of an online introductory paediatric physical examination skills course on students' OSCE performance.
citation: George Ann, Blaauw Duane, Dangor Ziyaad, Lala Sanjay G. (2025). Evaluation of the impact of an online introductory paediatric physical examination skills course on students’ OSCE performance. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08177-5
title: PPES online multimedia paediatric physical examination skills course
description: The Paediatric Physical Examination Skills (PPES) course is an online multimedia course on the University's Canvas instance (Ulwazi), consisting of five modules: General Examination, Vital Signs Measurement, Nutritional Assessment, Respiratory Distress and Noisy Breathing Assessment, and Assessment of Hydration and Perfusion. It includes narrated and unnarrated skills demonstration videos, audio recordings, clinical photographs, and infographics, with "the use of local South African patients and instructors in clinical settings in the videos". The recording sequence "approximates the first two steps of Peyton’s four-step teaching approach", with testing videos followed by feedback videos.
requirements: Hosted on the university learning management system; developed by paediatricians, a health professions educationalist, curriculum designers and instructional designers.
constraints: Videos range from 30 s to 5 min; the course was designed to introduce the basic paediatric examination and augment lecture-based and bedside teaching at the pre-clinical GEMP II level.
target_learning_goals: Core paediatric physical examination concepts and skills
examples: Students watched a non-narrated video, recorded their observations, then viewed narrated or text feedback videos; additional materials included bedside skills drill instructions, multiple-choice quizzes and downloadable PDFs.
key_sources: George Ann, Blaauw Duane, Dangor Ziyaad, Lala Sanjay G. (2025). Evaluation of the impact of an online introductory paediatric physical examination skills course on students’ OSCE performance. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08177-5

article_title: Clinical simulation for nurses' knowledge on postpartum hemorrhage: a randomized clinical trial.
citation: Coelho Tatiane da Silva, Fonseca Luciana Mara Monti, Cardoso Maria Vera Lúcia Moreira Leitão, Aquino Priscila de Souza, da Costa Camila Chaves, Maciel Nathanael de Souza, Damasceno Ana Kelve de Castro. (2025). Clinical simulation for nurses' knowledge on postpartum hemorrhage: a randomized clinical trial. Revista Brasileira de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/0034-7167-2024-0214
title: Validated PPH clinical simulation scenario (45-minute individual session: 5 min prebriefing, 10 min action, 30 min debriefing) with expected-actions checklist
description: A clinical simulation scenario on a postpartum hemorrhage case due to uterine atony, originally developed in 2016, validated by 22 UFPE faculty specialists, updated in 2022 to the revised WHO (2018) PPH protocol and revalidated by 22 specialists and the target audience. The scenario contained "1) General and specific objectives; 2) Competencies and skills; 3) Materials; 4) Case description; 5) Guiding questions for debriefing; 6) Checklist of expected actions". It was implemented individually with each nurse for 45 minutes (5 min prebriefing, 10 min action, 30 min debriefing).
requirements: Nurses were required to attend a PPH lecture beforehand, know the physiology and anatomy of labor, delivery and the immediate postpartum period, be familiar with the PPH treatment protocol, and understand biosafety resources and materials used
constraints: Evaluated in a single setting, the obstetric center of one tertiary maternity hospital
Knowledge retention was not assessed over time
target_learners: Registered nurses providing direct obstetric care in maternity hospital sectors
target_learning_goals: Knowledge and management competencies for postpartum hemorrhage, including clinical judgment, visual estimation of blood loss, shock index calculation, early diagnosis, calling for help, and initiating the medication protocol
examples: Each nurse underwent a handover by a nurse giving case details, then acted in the scenario, with the checklist recording whether actions were performed, correctly or incorrectly, and timely or delayed, followed by the structured debriefing
key_sources: Coelho Tatiane da Silva, Fonseca Luciana Mara Monti, Cardoso Maria Vera Lúcia Moreira Leitão, Aquino Priscila de Souza, da Costa Camila Chaves, Maciel Nathanael de Souza, Damasceno Ana Kelve de Castro. (2025). Clinical simulation for nurses' knowledge on postpartum hemorrhage: a randomized clinical trial. Revista Brasileira de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/0034-7167-2024-0214

article_title: When can we identify the students at risk of failure in the national medical licensure examination in Japan using the predictive pass rate?
citation: Shioiri Toshiki, Nakashima Michiyo, Tsunekawa Koji. (2024). When can we identify the students at risk of failure in the national medical licensure examination in Japan using the predictive pass rate? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05948-4
title: Predictive pass rate (PPR): a logistic-regression prediction formula for NMLE pass probability usable from admission onward
description: The PPR is a prediction formula for the pass rate of the NMLE built with logistic regression analysis at five time points (admission and the end of 1st, 2nd, 4th, and 6th grades), using 7 pre-admission and 10 post-admission variables. The article states it "created the PPR, which is a prediction formula, for the pass rate of NMLE using logistic regression analysis with all possible models". Students are divided into high (PPR < 95%) and low (PPR ≥ 95%) risk groups, and the PPR is used to identify students at risk of failure early and target intervention.
requirements: Requires pre-admission variables (e.g., gender, age at admission, HS location, GPA, NCTUA score) and, at later time points, post-admission academic performance variables available at each grade
constraints: The article notes "there are inherent pitfalls of using prediction models such as overfitting" and that applicability to other medical schools is not clear because no similar studies have been conducted elsewhere
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students in a 6-year Japanese medical program
target_learning_goals: Passing the National Medical Licensure Examination at the first attempt
examples: Seven consecutive cohorts (n = 637, 2012–2018) at Gifu University School of Medicine were classified into high- and low-risk groups at five time points and their movement simulated over 6 years
key_sources: Shioiri Toshiki, Nakashima Michiyo, Tsunekawa Koji. (2024). When can we identify the students at risk of failure in the national medical licensure examination in Japan using the predictive pass rate? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05948-4

article_title: Appropriate Delivery Project: Impact of Simulation Training on the Increase in Vaginal Births in Hospitals in Brazil.
citation: Molina Mariana Santos Alecrim, Cordioli Eduardo, Couto Thomaz Bittencourt, Barreto Joyce Kelly Silva, Sanchez Rita de Cássia. (2024). Appropriate Delivery Project: Impact of Simulation Training on the Increase in Vaginal Births in Hospitals in Brazil. Einstein (São Paulo). https://doi.org/10.31744/einstein_journal/2024AO0783
title: High-fidelity obstetric simulation training program of the Appropriate Delivery Project pilot
description: A theoretical-practical training program at a São Paulo simulation center, undertaken by 339 professionals (147 nurses, 192 physicians) from 27 hospitals. It combined a 4-hour theoretical module (obstetric safety, birth physiology and partograms, labor monitoring, assertive communication) with hands-on practice: "the use of patient simulators (SimMom - Laerdal®) during scenarios, static mannequins (Promp Birthing – Laerdal®; maternity simulation jacket - koken®)", professional actors in realistic facilities, and 10-minute team scenarios followed by 25-minute debriefings on dystocia, companions in the room, and cesarean-versus-vaginal indications.
requirements: Designed with the support of obstetrics experts and a realistic simulation center team
Approximately 38 students per class divided into four groups for active participation in rotating tasks
constraints: Conducted at a single simulation center in São Paulo, Brazil, during the pilot phase from May 21, 2015 to May 21, 2016
target_learners: Obstetricians providing obstetric care in the participating hospitals
target_learning_goals: Managing obstetric complications with patient safety and clinical reasoning
Directing proper delivery, monitoring labor, and stimulating the vaginal route
Communication skills including delivering bad news, conflict management, and encouraging adherence to prenatal care and normal delivery
examples: Scenarios lasting 10 minutes were transmitted to other group participants, followed by a 25-minute debriefing; tasks included cardiotocography case interpretation, postpartum hemorrhage management, pelvic birth maneuvers, forceps delivery, and vacuum extraction.
key_sources: Molina Mariana Santos Alecrim, Cordioli Eduardo, Couto Thomaz Bittencourt, Barreto Joyce Kelly Silva, Sanchez Rita de Cássia. (2024). Appropriate Delivery Project: Impact of Simulation Training on the Increase in Vaginal Births in Hospitals in Brazil. Einstein (São Paulo). https://doi.org/10.31744/einstein_journal/2024AO0783

article_title: Cognitive Style and Mobile E-Learning in Emergent Otorhinolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Disorders for Millennial Undergraduate Medical Students: Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Lee Li-Ang, Chao Yi-Ping, Huang Chung-Guei, Fang Ji-Tseng, Wang Shu-Ling, Chuang Cheng-Keng, Kang Chung-Jan, Hsin Li-Jen, Lin Wan-Ni, Fang Tuan-Jen, Li Hsueh-Yu. (2018). Cognitive Style and Mobile E-Learning in Emergent Otorhinolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Disorders for Millennial Undergraduate Medical Students: Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.8987
title: Conventional PowerPoint show (PPS) module of narrated video lectures for mobile e-learning
description: The control module in which "the learners chose and watched 10 visual-auditory text-image videos of emergent ORL-HNS disorders (a total of 80 min) by themselves". Videos were created by recording PowerPoint presentations with audio narrations, timings, and ink gestures using Camtasia Studio software, and learners could rewind and fast-forward as needed. It presents the same instructional slides as the IM module but arranged linearly, and represents a formal, serious learning modality in the article's terms.
requirements: Identical textbook-based instructional content to the IM module, confirmed equivalent by two investigators (r=.91, Spearman correlation)
constraints: The article describes it as a formal, serious learning modality that students found less satisfying than the gamified IM module
target_learners: millennial undergraduate medical students who are novices in ORL-HNS
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning competence for emergent ORL-HNS scenarios
examples: PPS learners used an app to read and listen to instructional materials in 10 linear-designed sessions on a 7-inch tablet for 100 min
key_sources: Lee Li-Ang, Chao Yi-Ping, Huang Chung-Guei, Fang Ji-Tseng, Wang Shu-Ling, Chuang Cheng-Keng, Kang Chung-Jan, Hsin Li-Jen, Lin Wan-Ni, Fang Tuan-Jen, Li Hsueh-Yu. (2018). Cognitive Style and Mobile E-Learning in Emergent Otorhinolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Disorders for Millennial Undergraduate Medical Students: Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.8987

article_title: "No patient should die of PPH just for the lack of training!" Experiences from multi-professional simulation training on postpartum hemorrhage in northern Tanzania: a qualitative study.
citation: Egenberg Signe, Karlsen Bjørg, Massay Deodatus, Kimaro Happiness, Bru Lars Edvin. (2017). “No patient should die of PPH just for the lack of training!” Experiences from multi-professional simulation training on postpartum hemorrhage in northern Tanzania: a qualitative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-0957-5
title: Multi-professional simulation design combining team training, skills training, realistic repeated scenarios, and debriefing with a systems approach to human error
description: The article's training design pattern for emergency obstetric care: small multi-professional teams (nurse midwives, doctors, medical attendants) train together on a birthing simulator after technical skills training, practicing realistic severe PPH scenarios aimed at prevention, management, and communication. Scenarios and debriefings are repeated so every trainee participates actively twice and observes twice, and debriefings encourage reflective learning on responsibility, guilt, and destiny in a confidential, safe environment. The authors conclude that "training in teams, skills training and realistic scenarios, repetition of scenarios with subsequent debriefing for reflective learning, were crucial for enhanced teamwork."
requirements: Training conducted in the local language with a contextual approach based on the locally established PPH protocol and the Helping Mothers Survive: Bleeding after Birth learning package
Debriefing within a confidential and psychologically safe environment facilitated so trainees can challenge their own habits and beliefs
constraints: The training was conducted at two northern Tanzanian hospitals; the pattern is situated in a low-resource maternity setting
examples: Teams practiced realistic and severe PPH scenarios on the MamaNatalie birthing simulator, with scenarios and debriefings repeated so all trainees participated actively twice and observed colleagues twice
key_sources: Egenberg Signe, Karlsen Bjørg, Massay Deodatus, Kimaro Happiness, Bru Lars Edvin. (2017). “No patient should die of PPH just for the lack of training!” Experiences from multi-professional simulation training on postpartum hemorrhage in northern Tanzania: a qualitative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-0957-5
